inline.s: If all the forms arise not, then the sense-organs are no organs;
Therefore, O World-Honored One, do you proclaim the organs and forms as “calamitous.”
“How, not comprehending form, does one yet have consciousness arise?
How, when consciousness arises not, does one yet undergo birth and death?”
“The sense-organs and their objects—the noble ones understand their meaning;
The foolish and the unwise vainly grasp and cling to their names.
One should not grasp the sixth, whether it be with grasping or without;
To be free of all defects, the noble ones speak no fixed teaching.
The sectarians, lacking in wisdom, are frightened of both ceasing and enduring;
They reckon the conditioned and the unconditioned as no different from a self.
Some reckon the self the same as mind; others hold it other than the mental;
The one-nature they take as graspable, and likewise the differing nature.
If the grasp is decisive understanding, it is then called mind and mental factors;
Why cannot this very grasp decisively understand the one nature?
With grasping and performance of deeds, one may then be reborn again;
As in what is produced by fire, the principle appears and yet appears not.
Just as when fire blazes up in a single instant, the kindling and the burnable are both present;
So too is the vain-grasped self—how then can there be no grasping?
Whether it is born or is not born, the nature of the mind is ever pure;
The self set up by the sectarians—why not take it as this very analogy?
In the dense forest of deluded consciousness, men falsely reckon apart from the true Dharma;
Delighting in theories of self, they run to and fro here and there.
That which is realized by inner awareness—the pure true mark of self—
This is the tathāgatagarbha, which the sectarians cannot know.
Discriminating among the skandhas, the grasping and the grasped:
If one can understand these marks, then true wisdom arises.
These sectarians, at the ground of the ālaya-storehouse,
Reckon the mental and a self together—this was not spoken by the Buddha.
If one can discern all this, one is released and sees the true reality;
The defilements of the path of vision and of practice, wholly cut away, are all purified.
The intrinsically pure mind is what beings deludedly grasp;
The undefiled tathāgatagarbha, far removed from the limit and the no-limit.
The primal consciousness within the skandhas, like gold and silver within the ore;
When it is smelted and refined, the gold and silver both appear.”
“The Buddha neither is a person nor is a skandha, but is only the undefiled wisdom,
Who comprehends the ever-quiet still—this is where I take my refuge.
The intrinsically pure mind, which follows the defilements, the mental, and the rest,
And which is in accord with a self—may the Buddha explain it.”
“The intrinsically pure mind, together with the mental and the rest as other;
The karmic accumulation they build, being defiled, is on that account twofold.
The mental and the rest, the defilements, stain the pure mind,
Just as a pure cloth is stained with all manner of grime.
As the cloth obtains separation from the grime, and as gold comes out of the ore;
The cloth and the gold are both unharmed; so is the mind that has left its faults.
The unwise seek and search after the lute, the drum, and the rest,
And yet hunt for a wondrous sound; so too within the skandhas is the self.
Like unto a hidden treasure, and like the water under the ground;
Though it exists, it cannot be seen; so too the true self within the skandhas.
The functions of mind and mental factors, gathered and conjoined with the skandhas:
The unwise cannot grasp them; so too the self within the skandhas.
As a woman carrying a child in the womb, though it exists she cannot see it;
The true self within the skandhas, the unwise cannot know.
As the potent force within medicine, and as the fire within the wood;
The emptiness within all dharmas, and likewise the nature of impermanence;
The sovereign mastery, the transcendent powers of all the stages, the highest samādhi of consecration—
Without this true self, all these are utterly nonexistent.
Some men object and say, “If it exists, you should show it to me”;
The wise should then reply, “You show me your own discrimination.”
One who denies the true self, slandering the Dharma, clings to both existence and nonexistence;
The bhikshu should hold an ordination and cast him out, no more speaking with him.
To proclaim the true self blazing, like the raging fire of a kalpa, is to
Burn away the dense forest of selflessness, and depart from the errors of all sectarians.
Like clarified butter, curds, and rock-candy, and the oils of sesame and the rest,
They all have taste, yet he who has not tasted them does not know.
Within all the aggregates of the body, seeking the self in five ways:
The fool cannot comprehend; the wise seeing is at once release.
The analogy established by the wise has not yet been made clear in the mind;
The meaning gathered within it—how could it make things understood?
The dharmas that are distinct and different, comprehended not as the one mind alone;
Those who reckon and calculate vainly grasp at what has no cause and no rising.”
“The one in absorption observes the mind, yet the mind does not see the mind;
The seeing is born from the seen; from what cause does the seen arise?”
“My lineage is Kātyāyana, born in the pure abode of the heavens;
I teach the Dharma for beings, so they enter the city of nirvāṇa.
Relying on the Dharma that abides primordially, I and all the Tathāgatas,
In the three thousand scriptures, have set forth the Dharma of nirvāṇa at length.
In the desire realm and in the formless realm, one does not there become a Buddha;
In the highest heaven of the form realm, one free of desire attains bodhi.
Realm is not the cause of bondage; it is bondage to the realm that binds;
Practice with the sharp sword of insight, and cut those defilements away.
If there is no self, how can the dharmas of illusion exist or not exist?
The fool should reveal the suchness itself—how can there be no true self?
The dharmas already made and not yet made, none of them arise from a cause;
All of them are entirely unarisen, which the foolish cannot comprehend.
The one who acts does not arise, nor do the acted-upon and all the conditions;
These two are both unarisen—how then can one reckon an agent?
Those who vainly reckon assert existence, whether prior, later, or simultaneous cause,
Like the potter's disciple and the rest, proclaiming how things are produced.
The Buddha is not the conditioned—what he possesses as all the marks and fine features,
Are the merits of a wheel-turning king; by these he is not called Tathāgata.
The Buddha takes wisdom for his mark, far from all views;
What is realized within through self-cognition, all faults are cut away.
The deaf, the blind, the dumb and the like, the aged and young, and those who bear resentment—
Such ones, being most heavily burdened, have no share in the holy life.
With the subtle features hidden he becomes a god, with the marks hidden a wheel-turning king;
But these two fall to heedless indulgence; only one who reveals them leaves the world.
After I, Shakyamuni, have passed away, there will arise Vyāsa,
And Kaṇāda, Ṛṣabha, and Kapila, and others.
A hundred years after my passing, what Vyāsa spoke,
The treatises of Bharata and the rest, and next the Sāṃkhyas.
Then Kaunḍinya the Brāhmaṇa, and next the king Mau-li,
Then Nanda and Guṇamati and the rest, and next the Mleccha kings.
Afterward arise the weapons of war, and next a time of utmost evil;
In that time all the world will not cultivate the true Dharma.
After such eras as these have passed, the world goes round as a wheel;
The sun and fire combining together will burn the desire realm.
Again the gods are established, and the world comes into being anew;
The kings and the four castes, the sages, spread the teaching of the Dharma.
The Vedas, sacrifices, and giving—then these doctrines will flourish;
Discourse, humor, and the arts of play, in prose and in commentary.
Hearing such things as these, the world is bewildered and confounded;
Of the various robes one receives, if they have a proper color,
Dyed with blue clay, with cow-dung and the like, so that they lose their brightness,
All the robes that one wears, to banish the marks of sectarians—
As it is shown to the practitioner, the banner-mark of all the Buddhas;
Also to bind the waist-cord, and to strain water before drinking.
Beg for alms in due order, and do not go to an improper place;
One is born in the highest wonderful heavens, and born again among humans.
One endowed with the precious marks is born among the gods and human kings;
The king who holds the four continents, long ruling by the Dharma.
Rising up to the heavenly palaces, all these are lost again through greed;
The era of pure virtue and the three times, the second times and the time of utmost evil.
Other Buddhas appear in a good age; Shakyamuni in an evil world;
After my nirvāṇa there is Siddhārtha of the Shākya clan.
Viṣṇu and Maheśvara, and the sectarians too, will all appear;
Thus have I heard and so forth, spoken by the teacher of the Shākyas.
Discourse on ancient tales and laughter, as spoken by the sage Vyāsa;
After my nirvāṇa, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara,
Will speak such words as this: “I am able to create the world.
My name is the Buddha Free of Dust; my family is Kātyāyana.
My father is the Lord of the World; my mother's name is Endowed with Wealth;
I am born in the land of Champa; my forefathers,
Born of the lunar lineage, are therefore called Moon-store;
I left home and practiced austerities, and proclaimed a thousand Dharma-gates,
Gave prophecy to Mahāmati, and then passed into quiescence.”
Mahāmati entrusted it to Dharma, and next he entrusted it to Mokṣa,
In the evil age of Mokṣa, when the kalpa ends, the Dharma will be extinguished.
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni,
And I, free of the dust, all appear in an age of pure virtue.
When the pure virtue gradually declines, there is a guide named Wisdom,
Who achieves great valor and courage, and awakens to the five dharmas;
Not in the second time, not in the third, nor in the time of utmost evil,
But in that age of pure virtue, he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Though the robe is not cut into threads, it is patched together from scraps,
Like the eye-spots of a peacock's tail, which no one can take away;
Or of two spans, of three spans, pieced together in alternation,
Whatever is made otherwise than this, the foolish cling to it in greed.
Keep only the three robes, always quenching the fire of greed,
Washing with the water of wisdom, practicing in the three divisions of the day and night;
As when an arrow's force is spent, it falls, and one lets fly another;
And as the churning-stick churns the curd, so are the wholesome and the unwholesome.
If the one can give rise to many, then there are distinct and different marks;
The giver should be as a field, the receiver as the wind;
If the one can give rise to many, then all things exist without a cause,
And the cause of the deeds, when destroyed, is a set-up of vain reckoning.
If it is a set-up of vain reckoning, like the lamp and the seed,
The one that gives rise to many is only similar, not truly many;
Sesame does not produce beans, and rice is not the cause of barley;
The small bean is not the seed of millet—how does the one give rise to many?
The name-maker composed the treatises on sound, the broad lord made the science of kings,
The materialists speak vainly and will be born in the Brahma-storehouse;
Kātyāyana wrote the scriptures, the bark-clad sage spoke of rites,
The owl brought forth astronomy—these will appear in an evil age.
The beings of the world, through the power of merit, are drawn to a king,
Who rules all things according to Dharma, and guards the land;
Blue-ant and the red-bean, the by-way and the horse-trader,
These great sages of merit will appear in the world to come.
Siddhārtha of the Shākya clan, Step-many and Five-coil,
The mouth-power and the wise—these too will come forth in the future.
While I dwelt in the forest and wilds, Brahmā the king came and gave me
The deer-skin, a three-pronged staff, an armband, and a water-pot;
This great practitioner will become the Lord free of dust,
Speaking on true liberation, the banner-mark of the Muni.
Brahmā and the Brahmā host, the gods and the heavenly hosts,
Gave me the deer-skin robe, and returned to the palace of freedom.
While I dwelt among the trees of the wood, Indra and the four heaven-kings
Gave me the wonderful robe, and also the bowl for begging.
If one sets up the doctrine of non-arising, then from cause there is birth again and again,
And one who sets up non-arising in this way is only uttering vain words.
What has been accumulated from the beginningless, ignorance is the mind's cause;
Birth and death continuing in succession is what vain reckoning discriminates.
The Sāṃkhya theory has two: the primordial matter and its evolution.
Within the primordial is what is made; what is made should arise of itself;
The primordial and the objects together, and the qualities proclaimed as differing.
The producer and the produced, in all their varieties, the evolution is never obtained;
As quicksilver is pure and clear, and dust cannot defile it,
The pure ālaya consciousness is the same—what beings rely upon;
As the scent of the asafetida and onion, salt-flavor, and the embryo's store.
Likewise the seed—how is it that it does not sprout?
The one nature and the different nature, the both and the neither, likewise.
It is not the existence that is grasped, not the nonexistence, not conditioned or unconditioned;
As the ox-nature is absent in the horse, so is the self within the skandhas.
What is spoken as conditioned and unconditioned is all without self-nature;
Seeking the self by reason and by scripture is a deluded and evil view.
Because they do not comprehend, they assert existence, only vainly grasping, nothing else;
The self within all the skandhas, whether one or different, is never established.
Those faults are evident, yet the vain-reckoning do not perceive it;
As water, mirror, and the eye manifest all manner of images.
Far from the one and the different, so is the self within the skandhas;
The practitioner who meditates in absorption, and sees the truth, and the path,
Practicing diligently these three, is released from all evil views;
As in a crevice one sees the lightning quickly vanish,
So too do dharmas pass away; one should not give rise to discrimination.
The foolish, deluded in mind, grasp at nirvāṇa as existence and nonexistence.
If one attains the noble vision, one is able to understand as it truly is;
One should know the dharmas of transformation, far removed from birth and death.
Also far from existence and nonexistence, and from the marks of subject and object;
One should know the dharmas of transformation, far from the sectarian theories.
Also far from names and marks, and the inner view of self is extinguished;
The gods delight in the touching of the body, the hells are pained by the body's affliction.
If there were no intermediate being there, all the consciousnesses could not arise;
One should know that in all the realms of birth, beings take the various bodies,
That womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born and the rest all follow the intermediate being;
Departing from the true principle of the noble teaching, seeking to quell delusion one only adds to it.
These are the wild words of sectarians; the wise should not speak them;
First one should resolve the self, and discriminate all the takings,
For like the barren woman's child, there is no resolving or discriminating.
I, apart from the fleshly eye, with the heavenly eye and the wisdom-eye,
See the bodies of all beings, apart from the activities and the skandhas:
Within the activities I see there is fair form and foul form,
Liberation and non-liberation, and those who dwell among the gods;
The bodies received in all the realms of birth—only I am able to realize them.
It transcends what the world knows, and is not the sphere of calculation;
With no self, the mind arises—how does this mind arise?
Has it not been said that the mind arises like the river, the lamp, and the seed?
If there were no ignorance and the rest, the consciousnesses would not arise.
Apart from ignorance there is no consciousness—how then does the continuation arise?
What the vain-reckoning speak of, the three times and that which is not of time,
Also the fifth that is ineffable—this is what the Buddhas know.
The activities dwelling in their grasp, and that too is the cause of wisdom;
One should not speak of wisdom and call it the activities.
Given this cause and this condition, then this dharma arises;
There is no other agent—this is what I have said.
The wind cannot produce fire, nor cause the fire to blaze brightly,
It is likewise by the wind that it is quenched—how does this serve as the analogy for self?
What is spoken as conditioned and unconditioned is all apart from the takings.
How do the foolish discriminate, using fire to establish a self?
It is by the mutual power of all the conditions, therefore, that fire is produced.
If one discriminates as with fire, then from whom is the self born?
With the mental and the rest as cause, the skandhas and sense-bases are gathered;
The merchant-leader of selflessness always arises together with the mind;
These two are ever like the sun, far from the agent and the deed.
Not fire can establish it; the vain-reckoning do not know;
Beings' mind, nirvāṇa, is intrinsically ever pure.
From beginningless past the stain of habit, without difference, like space;
The elephants' lying and the other sectarians are defiled by their various views.
Covered by the mano-consciousness, they reckon fire and the rest as pure;
If one obtains the vision of reality, then one is able to cut off affliction.
Forsake the dense forest of false analogies and reach where the noble ones roam;
The distinctions known by wisdom, each differently discriminated.
The unwise do not know, and speak of what should not be spoken,
As the foolish, seizing on an inferior wood, make of it sandalwood and aloe;
Vain reckoning and true wisdom—one should know that they too are the same.
When the meal is done, take up the bowl and return; wash it till it is clean,
Gargle and rinse the remaining taste of the mouth—one should thus cultivate.
If one, regarding this Dharma-gate, thinks rightly and in accord with principle,
With pure faith, free of discrimination, one achieves the highest samādhi;
Free from attachment, abiding in the meaning, one becomes the golden-light lamp of the Dharma.
Discriminating among existence and nonexistence, and the net of evil views,
The three poisons and all the rest are abandoned, and one receives the Buddha's hand of consecration.
The sectarians cling to an agent, to wanderers' ways, and to no-cause;
They are terrified of dependent arising, and fall to the cut-off view, bereft of the noble nature.
The fruits and retributions arising by transformation, called the consciousnesses and the mental;
The mental arises from the ālaya; the consciousness arises dependent on the manas.
The ālaya gives rise to all the minds, as the sea gives rise to its waves;
The habitual tendencies are its cause, arising in accord with the conditions.
An instant, [as links] chained together, grasping the sphere of one's own mind;
The manifold various forms and marks, from the mental faculty and the rest, the consciousness arises.
Through the beginningless evil habits, it arises as if there were an external realm;
What is seen is only one's own mind, which the sectarians cannot comprehend.
From that one, conditioning on that, there arises another consciousness;
Therefore all the views arise, and one revolves in birth and death.
All dharmas are like a dream and an illusion, a moon in water, a mirage, a castle in the air;
One should know that all dharmas are but one's own discrimination.
Right wisdom, relying on suchness, gives rise to all the samādhis;
Like the illusion-like Śūraṅgama and the like, differing in these ways.
One enters the stages, the sovereign mastery and the transcendent powers;
Achieving the illusion-like wisdom, all the Buddhas consecrate his head.
